channel.title: Albert Arnó — Writing
channel.description: Albert Arnó is a physician and the founder of onmedic, a Barcelona health-technology studio working in eHealth since 2000. Notes on building measurement software for the body.

item.title: Reading Apple Health without fooling yourself
item.description: Apple Health holds dozens of metrics from several devices, recorded at wildly different qualities. The skill is knowing which ones were measured and which were inferred.

item.title: Sleep stages from a wrist: what the device is really doing
item.description: Your watch reports deep, core and REM in minutes. A sleep lab needs electrodes on your scalp to do that. Here is what the wrist is actually inferring, and which parts of it you can trust.

item.title: Training load does not add up across sports
item.description: Triathletes have been summing swim, bike and run load for years. The arithmetic is tidy and the physiology does not support it. What a multisport load number can and cannot mean.

item.title: Critical swim speed: the only pool test worth repeating
item.description: Two time trials, one subtraction, and a threshold pace that actually holds up. Why CSS beats heart rate and perceived effort in the water.

item.title: The gait metric your phone already records
item.description: Walking asymmetry has been sitting in Apple Health for years, measured continuously, read by almost nobody. It is one of the few consumer metrics with real clinical grounding.

item.title: What a wrist can and cannot tell you about VO₂max
item.description: Your watch reports a VO₂max to one decimal place. It has never measured your oxygen consumption. Here is what the number actually is, and the one thing it is genuinely good for.

item.title: W′ balance, or what a match actually costs
item.description: Cyclists have said 'burning matches' for decades. W′ balance turns the metaphor into kilojoules you can watch drain and refill during a ride.

item.title: What I learned deleting 93% of my own website
item.description: AnalyticsZone had 15,004 URLs across eleven hostnames and almost no readers. Cutting it to about 1,100 pages on one host was the most useful thing I did all year.

item.title: Restarting this blog, seven years later
item.description: This site published 194 posts between 2012 and 2019, and I wrote none of them. Here is what it actually was, why it stopped, and what it is now.

item.title: The maths runs on your phone, and that costs me things
item.description: Computing sports metrics on the device instead of the server is easy to say in a privacy policy and harder to live with. What it actually forecloses.
